messages.author: 01b216d7e6cc0000
messages.subject: Using posteriors as priors
parts:
Dear blavaan users,
I want to test the structural validity of a translated questionnaire with 37 items that, according to theory, load on three dimensions. The sample size is small (n=52). This is why I would like to use a Bayesian CFA.
Some properties of the original questionnaire have been already assessed with a similar sample size (n=44) and the authors sent me their database.
My question is: how can I use that data for my analysis?
I could run a Bayesian CFA with that database and use the posterior distributions as priors but I don't know how to include them in the model specification.
I could also extract some statistics (for example the means and sd of items) and specify the priors as described in the blavaan manual.

Thank you very much for any advice!

Best regards,
Mauro

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
parts: I could run a Bayesian CFA with that database and use the posterior distributions as priors

This should be mathematically equivalent to using a noninformative prior and fitting the model to all N = 52 + 44 = 96 observations.  So you could just combine the samples. 

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
parts:
Mauro,

If you are seeing whether the current sample has similar properties to the previous sample, then you might also find a two-group model to be helpful. But you would probably also want to do a sensitivity analysis with the priors: at these sample sizes, I would guess that the priors of factor variances (and potentially other parameters) would have a sizable influence on the posterior.

Ed

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
parts:
Mauro,

You could indeed run a cfa on the original data, then use those posteriors to define priors for your new data. One challenge here would involve defining distributions for the priors of your new model: the posteriors for the original data could give you a mean/sd for your priors, but those posteriors are not necessarily normal at n=44. Another challenge might involve prior sensitivity: the priors you use for the original data can influence the posteriors, which would then influence the prior for the new data.

Ed

parts:
Dear Ed Merkle,
thank you very much for your answer!
With regard to the first challenge, I wondered if the posterior distributions could be used as they were in the analysis of my model but, if I have correctly understood your message, the only data that can be used are the parameters of the posteriors (for example, the estimated means and SDs). I thought that blavaan or JAGS or any other Bayesian software could use the whole posterior distributions. 
Is there a way in blavaan to visualize the shapes of the posterior distributions and specify the priors accordingly? For example, if the posterior distribution of a factor loading is asymmetric, could I specify an asymmetric prior?
With regard to the second challenge, I could specify the priors for the original data as suggested in the paper titled "blavaan: Bayesian Structural Equation Models via Parameter Expansion", for example by placing uniform priors on the items' standard deviations with lower bounds at 0 and upper bounds at the maximum possible standard deviation (all items have a likert response scale with five levels: 0-1-2-3-4).
Do you think that following the example described in the paper could overcome the challenge?

Sincerely,
Mauro

messages.author: 645e2b041ea2a63e
messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
parts:
Mauro,

The Bayesian software typically provides you with a full sample from each parameter's posterior distribution, but there are no guarantees that these distributions are normal or anything else. You could visualize the distributions with the plot function, something like

plot(fit, 1:4, "histogram")

where the "1:4" is for the first four model parameters.

Regarding the second challenge, uniform priors could be a good starting point, but the more general point is that the results may differ under other priors. You might try a sensitivity analysis using alternative sets of priors.

Ed

Mauro,

(Copying the blavaan list, in case this is helpful for somebody else...)

1. Regarding the nu prior, I don't have a specific opinion about the precision of .25: I don't know the data or the previous results of similar data. You might consider a sensitivity analysis where you vary the priors and see how results change.

2 & 3. This info can be found in the documentation:

?dpriors


Ed

2017-01-24 15:32 GMT+01:00 Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com>:
Mauro,

You could indeed run a cfa on the original data, then use those posteriors to define priors for your new data. One challenge here would involve defining distributions for the priors of your new model: the posteriors for the original data could give you a mean/sd for your priors, but those posteriors are not necessarily normal at n=44. Another challenge might involve prior sensitivity: the priors you use for the original data can influence the posteriors, which would then influence the prior for the new data.

Ed
